Ridgeline — front-end redesign · direction A of three · blind concepts

The Field Instrument

docs/design/direction-a-instrument.html — one self-contained file, real terrain, no build step.

This app computes Horn slope, Evans–Young curvature and anisotropic least-cost corridors — it is a scientific instrument, and the interface should say so without apology. The lineage is the avalanche bulletin, the NOAA chart, the aviation EFB: ordinal data, tabular numerals, a legend that never leaves the screen, and a confidence grade rendered in the same visual grammar as a caution light, not hidden in a markdown file. Nothing here is soft or rounded, because nothing about a 22° leeward bench at −12 °C is soft — the map is the chart, and every other element is an instrument plate docked to its edge, sized to its content, never floating over the terrain uninvited except the one thing that must: the data readout at the exact point you tapped.

Color

#0A0D0EGround — ink-black with a blue-green cast, not navy
#14191BPanel — the dock, the sheet, every HUD plate
#29373AHairline — cyan-biased, not neutral grey
#D9E2DEInk — phosphor bone, never pure white
#4FB2C4Accent — Sounding Cyan. Spent once: selection, live data

Semantic state (good / caution / critical) is a separate three-tone scale — #74A16E / #C99A3E / #BD5D4C — reused for both offline coverage and evidence grade, and never doubles as the accent.

Layout & risk

The map is the chart. Everything else is a docked plate sized to its own content — never a floating card that grows or shrinks the map underneath it.

The one risk: a permanent 300px desktop dock, not a drawer. The product audit correctly warns against a permanent sidebar "costing a third of the screen forever" — at 21% of 1440px this is under that bar, and it is load-bearing for the thesis: data density is a virtue here, not a cost to be hidden behind a hamburger. It ships with an explicit, labelled collapse control, not a forced default.

Kept, deliberately: the ConditionsBar's underlying logic — always visible, states its value, says Not set in caution tone rather than a silent default. Rebuilt in the new visual language (hairline cells, tabular mono, a real compass dial) rather than replaced.

Design discipline applied here

Neutrals are chosen, not inherited. Every grey in this file — hairlines, secondary ink, tertiary ink — carries a slight bias toward Sounding Cyan rather than sitting at true neutral, so the instrument reads as one material rather than "dark UI + one accent colour."

Circles are dials, not decoration. The one visual rule this direction does not bend is "nothing rounded." The two exceptions — the compass dial and the locate button — are true instrument knobs, not a stylistic rounding of a rectangle. Every panel, chip, cell and button keeps a hard edge.

State is never colour alone. The disabled bedding row carries a hatch pattern, reduced weight and a written reason, not just grey text. Every confidence chip carries a left stripe, a dot and the word. Offline tiles are solid / hatched / outline before they are green / amber / neutral.

Panels are flat, not frosted. HUD plates over the map use flat alpha and a hairline edge, never backdrop-filter: blur() — blur reads as software chrome; a hard edge on an unblurred plate reads as an instrument bezel.

To check on a real device before trusting this: whether the 300px dock survives a 390px phone without becoming the very rail the product audit already condemned — the mobile mock here docks a 262px sheet above the conditions cluster rather than over it, which is the one structural lesson from that audit this direction does keep; whether the compass-dial SVGs stay legible at 1x on a budget Android screen in direct sun; and whether the cyan accent holds enough contrast against the hillshade backdrop across a full range of real elevation data, not just this one Hocking Hills tile.
